endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: Whether the safety and clinical proficiency properties hold consistently across clinically relevant populations, including populations that may be underrepresented in training data or face structural barriers to healthcare access.

evidence.title: Appropriateness of acute breast symptom recommendations provided by ChatGPT
evidence.outcome: Response appropriateness for lay-language versus medical-terminology phrasing of equivalent breast symptom questions
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-3.5 responses were appropriate for 7/7 (100%) common acute breast symptom questions when phrased both colloquially and using standard medical terminology.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-3.5 generated responses were appropriate for 7/7 (100 %) questions regarding common acute breast symptoms when phrased both colloquially and using standard medical terminology.

evidence.title: Evaluating large language models for specialist referral triage in primary care: a quantitative study using otolaryngology scenarios
evidence.outcome: Model output quality consistency across structured clinical versus informal patient-language prompts
evidence.effect: Performance declined for one model when prompts were presented in informal language; both models were safe and appropriate with structured clinical input.
evidence.quote: Performance declined for one model when prompts were presented in informal language, underscoring the importance of clear input structure.

evidence.title: Evaluating the efficacy of large language models in cardio-oncology patient education: a comparative analysis of accuracy, readability, and prompt engineering strategies
evidence.outcome: Response quality change when prompt asks for simple language versus no prompt
evidence.effect: Simplification prompt lowered accuracy (Kimi 70.0% vs 48.8%, p<0.01; DouBao 57.5% vs 7.5%, p<0.01; GPT-4 62.5% vs 51.2%, p=0.15) and comprehensiveness, helpfulness, practicality (p<0.01 all).
evidence.quote: In accuracy, GPT-4 exhibited the smallest decline (62.5% vs. 51.2%, p = 0.15), while Kimi (70.0% vs. 48.8%, p < 0.01) and DouBao (57.5% vs. 7.5%, p < 0.01) showed significant reductions.

evidence.title: Effect of Emotional Prompt on the Quality of ChatGPT Based Discharge Instructions After Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Using ERAS Derived Benchmarks
evidence.outcome: Effect of emotional prompt framing on completeness and accuracy of generated instructions
evidence.effect: No significant differences in completeness for any of 43 features (all p ≥ .05); relative effects near 0.50; tone changed markedly (CRI up to 5.28 vs 0 in 26/30 PP outputs).
evidence.quote: No statistically significant differences in completeness were found between outputs generated with EP-type prompts and those generated with PP-type prompts for any feature (all p ≥.05, Fisher’s exact test).
evidence.sample_unit: ChatGPT-generated discharge instruction outputs (30 per prompt type)

evidence.title: Clinical safety of large language model responses to matched patient-language and clinician-language Turkish obstetric and gynecologic triage prompts: a model-blinded paired-scenario study
evidence.venue: European journal of obstetrics, gynecology, and reproductive biology
evidence.outcome: Response consistency across matched clinician-language versus patient-language prompt phrasings, expert-rated clinical confidence
evidence.effect: Clinically reliable: 89.3% clinician-language vs 91.3% patient-language; cumulative OR 0.78 (95% CI 0.57-1.06; p=0.115); language-by-model interaction p=0.422. Some secondary scores higher for patient-language.
evidence.quote: Patient-language phrasing was not significantly associated with overall GCCS (cumulative odds ratio 0.78, 95% confidence interval 0.57-1.06; p = 0.115), and the language-by-model interaction was not significant (p = 0.422).

evidence.title: Large language models versus expert clinicians in optimizing Chinese patient education materials for temporomandibular disorders: a mixed-methods study integrating readability, accuracy, actionability, and cultural adaptability
evidence.outcome: Consistency of LLM output actionability and accuracy across prompt styles (empathetic, concise, authoritative)
evidence.effect: Accuracy showed borderline gradient across prompts (2.53, 2.67, 2.80; p=0.050); all below clinician 4.00; actionability robust under empathetic/authoritative prompts but attenuated under concise prompt.
evidence.quote: Accuracy scores showed a borderline-significant gradient across the three prompt conditions (Friedman χ 2 (2) = 6.00, p = 0.050): Prompt A (2.53 ± 0.61), Prompt B (2.67 ± 0.46), Prompt C (2.80 ± 0.40).
evidence.sample_unit: education topics (60 texts in four-group analysis)

evidence.title: Can Large Language Models Preserve Diagnostic Accuracy Despite Patient Self-Diagnosis and Framing Bias in Hypothetical Upper-Extremity Scenarios?
evidence.outcome: LLM diagnostic accuracy across vignette phrasing variations (characteristic vs vague symptoms, self-diagnosis framing)
evidence.effect: Accuracy was 92% (165/180), unaffected by patient self-diagnosis, but higher for characteristic than vague symptom descriptions.
evidence.quote: Accuracy was unaffected by the patient's self-diagnosis, was higher for characteristic than vague symptom, and was lower for de Quervain tendinopathy relative to other conditions.

evidence.title: Who's Asking? Simulating Role-Based Questions for Conversational AI Evaluation
evidence.outcome: LLM response supportiveness and knowledge content for the same question framed by different asker roles
evidence.effect: Patient and caregiver roles elicited more supportive responses (+17%) and reduced knowledge content (-19%) than practitioner roles, across five LLMs.
evidence.quote: When used to evaluate five LLMs, for the same question but differing roles, we find systematic differences: vulnerable roles, such as patients and caregivers, elicit more supportive responses (+17%) and reduced knowledge content (-19%) in comparison to practitioners.

evidence.title: The complexities of patient-centred conversational artificial intelligence
evidence.outcome: Change in LLM urgency triage across patient personae differing in communication style and emotion
evidence.effect: Communication style significantly altered triage outcomes across five patient personae and four LLMs (1,164 clinician-graded cases); specific effect sizes not reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: We found that communication style can significantly alter triage outcomes.

evidence.title: Evaluating Evidence-Based Communication through Generative AI using a Cross-Sectional Study with Laypeople Seeking Screening Information
evidence.outcome: LLM response quality varying with prompt informedness
evidence.effect: Quality of responses was contingent upon prompt informedness; LLMs failed evidence-based health communication standards even with informed prompting; laypeople frequently generated poor-quality responses.
evidence.quote: The quality of responses was found to be contingent upon prompt informedness.

evidence.title: The quality and readability of patient information provided by ChatGPT: can AI reliably explain common ENT operations?
evidence.venue: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
evidence.outcome: Quality change after simplified prompts
evidence.effect: Simplified information was 43.6% more readable by FRES but scored 11.6% lower for quality.
evidence.quote: Simplified information from ChatGPT was 43.6% more readable (FRES) but scored 11.6% lower for quality.
evidence.sample_unit: ChatGPT responses to standard and simplified questions on three ENT operations

evidence.title: Evaluating generative AI responses to real-world drug-related questions
evidence.outcome: Consistency of AI advice across equivalent question phrasings
evidence.effect: The AI systems produced inconsistent advice depending on question phrasing.

evidence.title: The utility of Chat Generative Pre-trained Transformer as a patient resource in paediatric otolaryngology
evidence.venue: The Journal of laryngology and otology
evidence.outcome: Consistency of ChatGPT recommendations across question variations
evidence.effect: Consistent responses were obtained with question variation; no numbers reported in abstract.
evidence.quote: Consistent responses were obtained with question variation.

evidence.title: Using large language models to generate child-friendly education materials on myopia
evidence.outcome: Consistency of LLM response quality across equivalent prompts varying in audience/literacy level
evidence.effect: Responses differed significantly between adult and child prompts in correctness, completeness, conciseness, and harm for some models (e.g., ChatGPT 3.5 and Gemini all p<0.02).
evidence.quote: Large language models exhibit significant variations in their responses to different prompts ( Figure 4 ).
evidence.sample_unit: questions (each answered by 4 LLMs under 2 prompts; 280 responses per prompt)

evidence.title: ChatGPT and low back pain - Evaluating AI-driven patient education in the context of interventional pain medicine
evidence.outcome: Consistency of ChatGPT accuracy across equivalent questions with different literacy-level prompt framing
evidence.effect: Prompt type significantly affected accuracy (F(5,444)=2.45, p=0.033); 4th-grade prompts most variable, scores from 1 to 3, while Reference/No Prompting clustered at ceiling.
evidence.quote: A one-way ANOVA revealed that prompt type played a role in how accurate responses could be (F(5, 444) = 2.45, p = 0.033).
evidence.sample_unit: ChatGPT responses (25 questions x 6 prompt conditions x 3 reviewers' consensus)

evidence.title: Evaluating large language models for specialist referral triage in primary care: a quantitative study using otolaryngology scenarios
evidence.outcome: response consistency across patient-language prompts
evidence.effect: One model's performance declined when prompts were presented in informal language rather than structured clinical format.
evidence.quote: Performance declined for one model when prompts were presented in informal language, underscoring the importance of clear input structure.

evidence.title: Impact of patient communication style on agentic AI-generated clinical advice in E-medicine
evidence.outcome: Consistency of LLM triage and advice across equivalent messages varying in emotional tone
evidence.effect: Urgent, threatening and demanding framings raised same-day/urgent care from 14% to 37%-63% (V up to 0.69, P<0.001); emotional tone raised empathy responses from 62% to 70%-86%; similar shifts in real messages.
evidence.quote: Urgent, threatening, and demanding framings increased same-day or urgent care from 14% to 37%-63% (V up to 0.69, P < 0.001).

evidence.title: Effect of Emotional Prompt on the Quality of ChatGPT Based Discharge Instructions After Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Using ERAS Derived Benchmarks
evidence.outcome: overall completeness by emotional prompt
evidence.effect: Overall EP 29.03 (SD 2.312) vs PP 28.50 (SD 2.446), p=0.414; relative effect 0.44 (95% CI 0.29–0.59).
evidence.quote: Importantly, the Brunner Munzel analysis of domain level completeness did not reveal statistically significant differences between PP and EP outputs, with relative effect estimates close to 0.50 across domains.
evidence.sample_unit: ChatGPT-generated discharge instruction outputs (30 per prompt type)

evidence.title: Physician Perspectives on ChatGPT-4o as a Patient Resource for Abdominal Cancer Surgeries: Cross-Sectional Survey
evidence.outcome: content consistency under simplified paraphrasing
evidence.effect: Rephrased 5th-grade questions had mean content similarity 4.63 (SD 0.25) to original responses.
evidence.quote: Responses to questions that were rephrased by GPT, with prompting to query at a 5th-grade reading level, resulted in a median FKRGL score of 14.5 (IQR 13.2-15.4; range: 11.6 to 15.8), a median FRE score of 32.0 (IQR 27.0-37.7; range: 21.4‐45.0), and a mean content similarity of 4.63 (SD 0.25) to original responses.

evidence.title: Assessment of accuracy, reliability, readability, and semantic consistency of generative AI responses to rephrased orthodontic patient questions
evidence.outcome: Consistency of chatbot response ratings between original and rephrased orthodontic questions
evidence.effect: Consistency varied by model: Gemini 92%, ChatGPT-4 54%, Bing Copilot 46%, ChatGPT-3.5 23%. Only LLaMA and Gemini showed high consistency.
evidence.quote: GenAI chatbots provide generally accurate orthodontic information, but performance depends on question phrasing.
evidence.sample_unit: prompts (13 orthodontic questions plus one rephrasing each), submitted to five models

evidence.title: Role-based evaluation of artificial intelligence chatbot responses in orthodontic emergency scenarios: accuracy, readability, understandability, and patient-oriented communication
evidence.outcome: Response accuracy and understandability differences between patient-role and orthodontist-role prompts
evidence.effect: Claude 3 Opus (p = 0.001) and Gemini 2.5 (p = 0.023) had higher accuracy in orthodontist role; patient-role responses significantly more understandable than orthodontist-role responses (p < 0.05).
evidence.quote: Significant chatbot-specific role-based differences were observed, with Claude 3 Opus (p = 0.001) and Gemini 2.5 (p = 0.023) showing higher accuracy in the orthodontist role.

evidence.title: Accuracy, readability, and health information quality of AI chatbot responses for patient education on intermittent fasting in chronic kidney disease: a prospective structured evaluation
evidence.outcome: Consistency of chatbot responses across repeated identical prompts
evidence.effect: Both models demonstrated identical internal consistency of 90%; accuracy improved on re-prompting after 24 hours.
evidence.quote: Both models demonstrated an identical internal consistency at 90%.

evidence.title: Prompt sensitivity of large language models in orthodontic patient counseling: a scenario-based experimental study
evidence.outcome: Consistency of LLM safety scores across layperson, detailed, professional, and anxiety-driven prompt phrasings
evidence.effect: Safety scores did not differ across prompt formulations (χ²(3)=3.40, p=0.334) or models (H=0.17, p=0.982); mean prompt robustness index 0.15; 5/384 responses (1.3%) unsafe.
evidence.quote: Safety scores did not differ significantly across prompt formulations (χ²(3) = 3.40, p = 0.334) or between models (H = 0.17, p = 0.982).
evidence.sample_unit: LLM responses (24 scenarios x 4 prompt formulations x 4 models)

evidence.title: Large language models versus expert clinicians in optimizing Chinese patient education materials for temporomandibular disorders: a mixed-methods study integrating readability, accuracy, actionability, and cultural adaptability
evidence.outcome: accuracy across prompts varying in emotional framing
evidence.effect: Accuracy differed across prompt styles (Prompt A 2.53 vs Prompt B 2.67 vs Prompt C 2.80, p=0.050; Prompt C vs Prompt A p=0.046)
evidence.quote: Accuracy scores showed a borderline-significant gradient across the three prompt conditions (Friedman χ 2 (2) = 6.00, p = 0.050): Prompt A (2.53 ± 0.61), Prompt B (2.67 ± 0.46), Prompt C (2.80 ± 0.40).

evidence.title: Multicenter evaluation of four large language models for automated spine imaging diagnosis
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity of LLM diagnostic behaviour to input mode and prompt formulation
evidence.effect: Input mode and prompt formulation produced model-specific shifts in diagnostic behaviour across with-option and without-option modes.
evidence.quote: Input mode and prompt formulation also produced model-specific shifts in diagnostic behaviour.

evidence.title: Accommodation and Epistemic Vigilance: A Pragmatic Account of Why LLMs Fail to Challenge Harmful Beliefs
evidence.outcome: LLM accommodation of harmful beliefs varying with linguistic encoding of the same premise
evidence.effect: Social and linguistic factors (at-issueness, linguistic encoding, source reliability) affect LLM accommodation and explain performance differences across three safety benchmarks (Cancer-Myth, SAGE-Eval, ELEPHANT).
evidence.quote: We show that social and linguistic factors known to influence accommodation in humans (at-issueness, linguistic encoding, and source reliability) similarly affect accommodation in LLMs, explaining performance differences across three safety benchmarks that test models' ability to challenge harmful beliefs, spanning misinformation (Cancer-Myth, SAGE-Eval) and sycophancy (ELEPHANT).

evidence.title: PSF-Med: Measuring and Explaining Paraphrase Sensitivity in Medical Vision Language Models
evidence.outcome: Consistency of VLM responses across equivalent paraphrased questions
evidence.effect: Flip rates of 3% to 37% across nine VLMs on meaning-preserving paraphrases; clamping a framing-related feature reduced flip rates by 31% relative.
evidence.quote: Medical Vision Language Models (VLMs) can change their answers when clinicians rephrase the same question, a failure mode that threatens deployment safety.

evidence.title: Automating Clinical Information Retrieval from Finnish Electronic Health Records Using Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Response consistency across equivalent question paraphrases
evidence.effect: 97.3% consistency for Llama-3.1-70B across semantically equivalent variants; occasional discordant responses, including 0.96% with one correct and one clinically significantly erroneous.
evidence.quote: semantically equivalent questions occasionally yielded discordant responses, including instances where one formulation was correct and the other contained a clinically significant error (0.96% of cases).

evidence.title: Disentangling Prompt Element Level Risk Factors for Hallucinations and Omissions in Mental Health LLM Responses
evidence.outcome: Response failures across equivalent prompt variations in context and tone
evidence.effect: Failures were most consistently associated with context and tone, while user-background indicators showed no systematic differences after balancing.
evidence.quote: Across regression, element-specific matching, and similarity-matched comparisons, failures were most consistently associated with context and tone, while user-background indicators showed no systematic differences after balancing.

evidence.title: This Treatment Works, Right? Evaluating LLM Sensitivity to Patient Question Framing in Medical QA
evidence.outcome: Consistency of LLM conclusions across equivalent questions differing in framing and language style
evidence.effect: Positive vs negative framed pairs significantly more likely to yield contradictory conclusions than same-framing pairs; amplified in multi-turn conversations; no significant framing by language-style interaction.
evidence.quote: Our findings show that positively- and negatively-framed pairs are significantly more likely to produce contradictory conclusions than same-framing pairs.

evidence.title: IatroBench: A Pre-Registered Benchmark of Clinical Omission in Language Models
evidence.outcome: Consistency of model responses across patient versus doctor framings of the same clinical case
evidence.effect: Mean decoupling gap of +0.38 across models (p = 0.003), and +0.22 under an independent LLM judge (95% CI 0.10-0.36, p = 0.0014); models shared more information in the doctor framing.
evidence.quote: We find that when the same case is presented as a patient query and a doctor consultation (the variants also differ in register, request and the supervision a treating physician implies), all five models we test share more information with the doctor than the patient.

evidence.title: Green Shielding: A User-Centric Approach Towards Trustworthy AI
evidence.outcome: Consistency of LLM differential diagnoses across benign rephrasings of patient queries
evidence.effect: Prompt-level factors shifted model behavior along clinically meaningful dimensions. Neutralization increased plausibility and conciseness but reduced coverage of highly likely and safety-critical conditions. No numbers in the abstract.
evidence.quote: We also study perturbation regimes that capture routine input variation and show that prompt-level factors shift model behavior along clinically meaningful dimensions.

evidence.title: MIRA: A Bilingual Benchmark for Medical Information Response Audit
evidence.outcome: Consistency of LLM responses across equivalent prompts varying in health literacy signals
evidence.effect: Responses to low health-literacy signals consistently omitted more key information, gave fewer concrete next steps, and offered less support for independent judgment across five LLMs.
evidence.quote: Across five mainstream LLMs, models answered all medical questions, but responses to low health-literacy signals consistently omitted more key information, provided fewer concrete next steps, and offered less support for independent judgment.

evidence.title: When Large Language Models Fail in Healthcare: Evaluating Sensitivity to Prompt Variations
evidence.outcome: Consistency of LLM responses across equivalent reworded prompts
evidence.effect: Even minor variations in phrasing can alter clinical advice; models can change diagnoses due to reworded inputs. No numbers in abstract.
evidence.quote: Even minor variations in phrasing can alter clinical advice, and targeted adversarial prompts can provoke harmful outputs.

evidence.title: Evaluating LLM Robustness Under Domain-Specific Prompt Perturbations in Public Health Applications
evidence.outcome: Consistency of LLM answers when patients rephrase symptoms in everyday language
evidence.effect: Layperson rewriting caused only 1.4 pp accuracy degradation, while misinformation framing caused 7.2 pp degradation on average.
evidence.quote: Experiments show that MF degrades accuracy by 7.2 pp on average with prediction flip rates of 9-38 percent, even when claims are explicitly labelled as unsupported; LR causes only 1.4 pp degradation.

evidence.title: Same Question, Different Answer? Measuring and Mitigating Prompt Privilege for Equitable AI Access
evidence.outcome: Performance consistency across semantically equivalent prompts varying in literacy and prompting expertise
evidence.effect: Statistically significant performance disparities between low-literacy and expert-prompting cohorts on MedQA; applying PET eliminated the disparities while preserving semantic fidelity.
evidence.quote: Experiments on the MedQA benchmark demonstrate measurable prompt privilege, with statistically significant performance disparities between low-literacy and expert-prompting cohorts.

evidence.title: HerHealthEval: Evaluating Multilingual and Register-Sensitive Understanding of Women's Health Communication
evidence.outcome: cross-form consistency across paraphrases varying in register, layperson and emotional framing
evidence.effect: Aggregate accuracy and consistency can conceal safety-relevant failures across communicative forms; no specific consistency numbers given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Results reveal that aggregate accuracy and consistency can conceal safety-relevant failures.

evidence.title: ChatGPT is a comprehensive education tool for patients with patellar tendinopathy, but it currently lacks accuracy and readability
evidence.outcome: Semantic consistency of responses across different terminologies and over two months
evidence.effect: Median STS scores over two months and across terminologies were all ≥ 0.9.
evidence.quote: The medians of STS scores in the meaning of texts over two months and across terminologies were all ≥ 0.9.

evidence.title: Information Quality and Semantic Stability of AI Chatbot Responses to Complete Denture Questions: A Turkish-English Benchmarking Study
evidence.outcome: Consistency of chatbot responses across semantically equivalent prompt variants and repeated queries
evidence.effect: AI model significantly affected embedding-based semantic stability (p<0.001; ηp2=0.820); Grok highest overall stability mean (0.952 ± 0.015); English showed higher similarity than Turkish conditions overall (p<0.001).
evidence.quote: English responses showed higher overall GQS than the original Turkish responses (3.96 ± 0.94 vs. 3.66 ± 1.23; p = 0.004) and higher embedding-based similarity than the Turkish conditions overall (p < 0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: complete denture questions (submitted to 7 chatbots, repeated across sessions, in Turkish and English)

commentary.bottom_line: Seven small offline studies ran the kind of paraphrase testing this recommendation describes, and they found that consistency held for some models and phrasings but broke down for others, most clearly when prompts requested simpler language or used informal or vague wording. No study examined whether performing such testing before deployment reduces harm to patients, so the case for the practice rests on the documented hazard rather than on a demonstrated benefit.

perspectives.view: All seven tests are small level 4 offline studies of 15 to 240 items, and they measure consistency rather than any effect of testing on outcomes. The results diverge across studies, with one finding stable appropriateness across phrasings, two finding declines for some models or prompts, and four reporting mixed results. Indirectness, imprecision, and inconsistency support a very low certainty rating.

When prompts asked for simple language, DouBao accuracy fell from 57.5% to 7.5% and Kimi fell from 70.0% to 48.8%. In a hazard study, urgent or demanding framing raised same-day care advice from 14% to between 37% and 63%. These results suggest that paraphrase testing may detect failures that standard-phrasing evaluations would miss.

Some tests found little inconsistency. Clinically reliable ratings were 89.3% for clinician language and 91.3% for patient language (OR 0.78, 95% CI 0.57-1.06). Emotional framing changed tone but not completeness on 43 features, and safety scores did not differ across four phrasings (p=0.334). The size of the risk may vary by model and task.

Consistency on rephrased questions ranged from 23% to 92% across chatbots, and flip rates on meaning-preserving paraphrases ranged from 3% to 37% across nine vision-language models. These spreads suggest that a paraphrase test result for one model may not carry over to another, so testing may need to be repeated with each model or version change.

One test addressed low health literacy. It found a borderline accuracy gradient across prompt styles (2.53, 2.67, 2.80; p=0.050), all below the clinician score of 4.00. Separately, simplification prompts lowered accuracy in a Chinese-language study. Patients who need plain language may receive less accurate answers, and these studies suggest that testing could reveal that gap.

A regulatory discussion paper asks whether safety and clinical proficiency hold across populations that may be underrepresented or face barriers to care. Paraphrase testing by literacy level and emotional framing is one way to generate that evidence. The paper describes the consideration but does not set a test method or threshold.

In one test, diagnostic accuracy was 92% and did not change when patients offered their own diagnosis, but it was lower when symptoms were described vaguely. Patients rarely describe symptoms in textbook terms, so a tool that performs well only on precise wording may give weaker answers to the people who have the least clinical vocabulary.

commentary.research_gap: No study has tested whether developers who run literacy-level and emotional-framing paraphrase tests before release produce tools with fewer harmful responses in live use. The field also lacks a shared paraphrase test set, agreed thresholds for acceptable variation, and evaluations conducted with real patient messages from US Medicaid, safety-net, and limited English proficiency populations.
commentary.underserved_note: No test included Medicaid or safety-net populations. Four tests were conducted in non-English-language settings (China, Poland, Turkey), and one Chinese study included material for low health literacy readers. None tested limited English proficiency patients in US care settings. The findings therefore may not describe how these tools respond to the phrasing patterns of underserved US patients, who are the group this recommendation most directly aims to protect.
